summary: This RFC describes a Telnet option for avoiding a double login. It is meant mainly for connections made by terminal access controllers on behalf of users, but any two hosts can use it. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: You show your ID at the first door, and a note tells the second door who you are, so you do not have to show it twice.

questions: how to avoid double login with telnet
what is the tacacs user identification telnet option
what is the telnet tuid option
how does telnet avoid double login
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets a terminal access controller pass along a user's proven identity so the target host can skip a second login.

tldr.problem: Under TACACS a user must authenticate to a TAC before connecting to a host through it, and the target host would then ask for a login again.
tldr.mechanism: The TUID Telnet option, option code 26, lets the user's side send a 32-bit UUID for the user in a subnegotiation, after both sides agree with WILL and DO.
tldr.outcome: Hosts may accept the TAC's authentication or not, at their option. The RFC is a proposed protocol that asks for discussion.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 927 as a Proposed Standard, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Avoiding a Double Login
sections.content:
Under TACACS (the TAC Access Control System) a user must give a correct name and password pair to a TAC before he can connect to a host via the TAC. To avoid a second authentication by the target host, the TAC can pass along the user's proven identity, his UUID, to that host. Hosts may accept the TAC's authentication of the user or not, at their option.

The option is intended mainly for TAC connections made for TAC users, but it can be used between any two consenting hosts, for example all hosts at one site.
sections.eli5: The first door already checked your ID, so it tells the second door your ID number and you can walk right in.

sections.title: The TUID Option Commands
sections.content:
The option is named TUID and has code 26. It uses the usual Telnet commands:

  • IAC WILL TUID: the user side proposes to authenticate the user and send the UUID, or agrees to do so.
  • IAC WON'T TUID: the user side refuses.
  • IAC DO TUID: the server proposes that the user side authenticate and send the UUID, or agrees to accept it.
  • IAC DON'T TUID: the server refuses to accept the authentication.
  • IAC SB TUID <uuid> IAC SE: the user side sends the UUID, a 32 bit binary number.

By default a host that does not implement the option answers WON'T TUID to a DO, or DON'T TUID to a WILL.
sections.eli5: The two computers ask each other yes or no questions first. Only if both say yes does the ID number get sent.

sections.title: Negotiation Cases and Encoding
sections.content:
Either side can start. In case 1 the server sends DO and the user replies WILL, and in case 2 the user sends WILL first and the server replies DO. In both, the user then sends the UUID by subnegotiation. If one side lacks the option, the answer is WON'T or DON'T and no authentication happens.

The UUID is sent as four octets. A value of 1 goes out as IAC SB TUID 0 0 0 1 IAC SE. A byte of value 255 has to be doubled, so the value 255 goes out as IAC SB TUID 0 0 0 IAC IAC IAC SE, and all ones goes out as eight IAC octets between TUID and the final IAC SE.
sections.eli5: Both must agree before the ID is sent, and some special number values are written in a doubled way so they are not mistaken for commands.
